The 12 grapes of New Year’s Eve
It’s 31 December. Mihai is spending New Year’s Eve with Ana’s family in Madrid. Grandma Rosario explains the tradition.
Mihai, here, these are your twelve grapes.
In Spain, on New Year’s Eve, you eat one grape on each chime of the clock at midnight. That’s how you welcome the New Year.
And if you eat them all in time, you’ll have luck all year.
Twelve grapes in twelve seconds? That’s impossible!
Ha, ha. All foreigners say the same thing. You have to eat them quickly, but carefully.
And in Romania? How do you celebrate New Year’s Eve?
People usually have dinner with family or friends, and at midnight they toast with champagne.
And there are some lovely traditions: children go from house to house with a decorated plough, singing to wish everyone a good year.
How lovely! Here, on the other hand, children get their presents on the sixth of January, on Three Kings’ Day.
Careful! The quarter chimes are starting… Now, the bells!
(with his mouth full) Mmmf… Ten, eleven, twelve! I did it!
Mihai, welcome to the family. This year is going to be very special, I know it.

Adverbs in -mente keep the adjective’s stress AND stress “MEN”: rá-pi-da-MEN-te, nor-mal-MEN-te.
Watch the difference: año (year) = “a-nyo”; ano (without ñ) is a rude word. Pronounce the ñ clearly!
Champán = “cham-PAN”, stressed on the last syllable.
1. Traditions with “SE”: how things are done
To describe traditions (what people do in general), the impersonal “se” from chapter 24 is perfect:
At Christmas people sing and dance.
On the Day of the Dead, graves are decorated with flowers.
Remember: plural thing → plural verb: se come una uva / se comen doce uvas.
To turn an adjective into an adverb (“quick” → “quickly”), you add -MENTE to the FEMININE form of the adjective. It’s like English “-ly”:
If the adjective has a written accent, it keeps it: rápido → rápidamente, fácil → fácilmente.
When you have two adverbs in a row, only the last one takes -mente: “lenta y cuidadosamente” (slowly and carefully).
Aquí se come turrón, mientras que allí se come cozonac.

Lena had heard about the Fallas in Valencia many times, but she had never seen them. In March she finally went with Tom and Javier, who is from Valencia.
They arrived on the evening of the fifteenth of March. The first thing they noticed was the noise: firecrackers everywhere, at all hours.
“Nobody sleeps here during the Fallas,” Javier explained, laughing.
The next day they walked around the city. In every square there was a “falla”: a huge figure of cardboard and wood, some as tall as a five-storey building.
There were fallas with politicians, footballers, film characters… They were all very funny and very critical.
Javier told them that the artists work for a whole year to build them.
At two in the afternoon they went to the Town Hall Square to see the “mascletà”. Lena thought it was a fireworks display, but there were no lights at all.
It was pure noise: thousands of firecrackers exploding in perfect rhythm, like wild music. The ground was shaking. Lena covered her ears, but she couldn’t stop smiling.
In the afternoon they watched the flower offering. Thousands of “falleras”, in gorgeous traditional dresses, carried flowers to the Virgin. All the flowers were used to make a giant cloak.
Some older women were crying with emotion. Lena was moved too, although she didn’t really understand why.
On the last night, the nineteenth of March, came the “cremà”: at midnight they burned all the fallas.
Lena watched sadly as the fire destroyed a whole year’s work in a few minutes. “Why do they burn them?”, she asked Javier. “They’re gorgeous.”
“That’s exactly why,” he answered. “So we can start again. The old is burned and spring arrives.”
They went back to Madrid exhausted, their ears still ringing. On the train Lena wrote in her notebook: “The Fallas can’t be explained. You have to live them.”
A month later Lena received a parcel from Valencia. It was from Javier. Inside was a little cardboard figure: a German girl with a guitar and a black cat.
A note said: “We won’t burn this one. It’s so you come back next year”. Lena put it on the shelf next to her books. She already knew she would go back.
Lluvia, the cat, looks at it suspiciously every day.
